Imagined art — the loaf on the cloth, not a photograph of one kitchen The loaf on the table A round loaf, cut thick. Salt on the same cloth. That is still the picture a lot of people mean by masă, the table, even when the rest of the meal is soup, cheese, or leftover stew. Guests are met with pâine și sare — bread and salt — a welcome older than any printed menu. You break, you salt, you sit. The word itself is Latin that stayed: pâine from panis, the same bone as the lesson on the Latin that stayed . Mămăligă sits beside the loaf in many houses and is not a lesser claim; it is a different one. Cornmeal is weekday filling. Bread is the sign that someone kept the room. Imagined art — colindători at the door, not a photograph House to house Colindători stop at the gate or the door and sing. The household that still keeps the custom does not leave them on the step. A glass, a piece of cake or a colac, coins, nuts, an apple — whatever the table can spare after the fast. Children come in a small pack, a parent a few yards behind. In some villages a company of young men still walks the street as a set that knows which yards will open. Town blocks hear less of this. The year page already said the true thing: they still walk some streets. Steaua, and the plough A few visits have names. pages.text: Pictures Traditions and craft What the hands still make. Quilting is here, and so are the older textile and wood trades around it. The blouse, the towel, the cover The ia is the embroidered blouse. The stitch, the sleeve, and the color mark a region more reliably than a postcard. A ștergar is a woven or embroidered towel, hung on an icon corner or offered to a guest. A cuvertură is a coverlet for the bed. Some of these are woven in one piece. Some are pieced from older cloth, which is the nearest thing in the house to what English calls a quilt. Romanian villages did not build the American block-quilt tradition. They did piece, patch, and layer wool and hemp covers against winter. If you are looking for quilting, start with the bed cover and the rag rug, not with a shop pattern. pages.title: Dance
pages.description: Hora. The circle the whole room can enter — hands already joined, a wedding yard or a feast, before anyone has decided they can dance. Not a stage. Not a list of steps.
pages.text: Home Dance Hora. The circle the whole room can enter — hands already joined, a wedding yard or a feast, before anyone has decided they can dance. Not a stage. Not a list of steps. The circle The hora is the dance people mean when they say the room stood up. Hands joined. A closed ring, or one that has not quite closed. The step is small enough that someone who has watched from a chair can take a place without a lesson. It can start almost at a walk. It can pull until the ring leans. There are horas named by village or by tune; this page does not list them. The fact is the same: the floor became a circle, and the circle took whoever would hold on. Cousins, not a catalog The sârba is faster. Same floor, a tighter count, men more likely to stamp. If the hora is how the yard says it is together, the sârba is how that yard gets warm. They often sit in the same evening, the slower circle…

It splits. Arms, canals, lakes that look like land until you try to walk them. People say Delta Dunării when they mean that maze, not the industrial water that passes Galați, not the tourist stretch near the Iron Gates. Those are still Dunărea. This is the place where the river becomes a country of its own: stuf, the reed, higher than a person; a boat that is the road; willows standing in water. pages.title: Dialects
pages.description: How Romanian actually varies, without pretending every village is a separate language.
pages.text: Words Dialects How Romanian actually varies, without pretending every village is a separate language. The Romanian you hear on the news, in school, and in a Bucharest shop is a standard. It was built, from the nineteenth century on, mostly on the speech of Wallachia, the southern dialect often called Muntenian, with choices from the written tradition and from the need to have one language for a new state. A standard is a decision. It is not the only way the language is spoken, and it is not more “correct” in a village than the speech people learned at home. It is the version with a dictionary, a spelling, and a microphone. Inside Romania, linguists usually group the older regional speech into a handful of dialects rather than a hundred. Șotron Play șotron Hopscotch. Chalk or a stick in the dust draws the boxes, numbered, usually ending in a half-circle people call the heaven or the house. You throw a flat stone, hop on one foot, and pick the stone up without putting the other foot down. If you land on a line or on both feet where you should not, you are out of that turn. Girls keep this one longer than boys in a lot of towns. The pattern on the ground is the same game your grandmother would recognize, even when the chalk is pink. Imagined art — the cut in the oak, not a photograph of one poartă Not a latch on a fence A poartă maramureșeană stands at the entrance to a household yard. Two posts, a lintel, a small roof of șindrilă, and often a side door for people while the main span is wide enough for a cart. You walk under it. You do not squeeze through a gap in boards. pages.text: Home Harvest Recoltă, and for wheat seceriș. Not a festival poster. The weeks when the field finishes and the cellar starts to matter more than the porch. Imagined art — grapes, maize, and the jars, not a photograph of one harvest Imagined art — what the harvest still feeds Wheat and the sickle memory Seceriș is the cutting of the grain. In living memory that meant bent backs, a sickle or a scythe, and neighbors who came for a day and were fed at noon under a tree. Combines do most of the work now where the fields are large enough, but the word stayed. People still say “am secerat” the way they say “we finished,” even when the machine did the finishing. Bundles, stacks, threshing on a hard floor — those pictures belong to grandparents more than to a teenager with a phone. What remains is the smell of cut straw, the hurry before rain, and the quiet after the last load leaves the plot…

pages.text: Home Honey Miere. Yard food and a gift, not a product line. The jar that still leaves a house wrapped in a cloth, or sits by the loaf with a spoon in it. The stup at the edge The hive sits where the orchard thins, or behind the house, past the woodpile and the hens. A stup, sometimes two, painted, a little leaning. Albine work the same air the yard already uses. Children are told not to stand in the line of the entrance. The dog learns. The well, the gate, the stove — those rooms are on the house . The road those yards share is on villages . This page is only that box at the edge, and what comes out of it. On the table Honey sits where bread sits. A round loaf, a knife, a spoon of miere instead of jam, or with the jam — that loaf is on bread . Tea with a spoon in it when someone coughs: not a pharmacy, the jar that was already in the cupboard. Winter opens it more often than July does…

pages.description: What people mean by casă when they are not talking about an apartment block. A yard, a gate, a stove, and the rooms that still hold the year.
pages.text: Home The house What people mean by casă when they are not talking about an apartment block. A yard, a gate, a stove, and the rooms that still hold the year. Yard first The house faces the yard more than the street. A fence or a carved wooden gate, the poartă, marks the edge. In Maramureș the gate can be taller than the house and carved with rope and sun and a short prayer — that monument is on gates . Elsewhere it is plainer: boards, a latch, a dog who knows who belongs. Inside the fence sit the well if there is one, the woodpile, a shed for tools, and often a small summer kitchen so the main room does not take the heat of every meal. Chickens still walk through a lot of these yards. The lawn is not the point. Space to work is. pages.text: Learn Romanian 3. Food and the table What you ask for, and what you say before you eat. Pâine is bread, the ordinary food of the table. In Moldavian and much Transylvanian speech you will hear pâne , without the i. The spelling stays pâine. Apă is water. Still water in a shop is apă plată ; sparkling is apă minerală . Brânză is cheese in general; telemea is the salty white kind. At the table: poftă bună before a meal, said to the people eating, including yourself. The reply is often the same, or mulțumesc . Noroc when glasses meet. O cafea, vă rog is a coffee, please. When you want the bill, nota, vă rog . A few kitchen words travel: sare salt, lapte milk, carne meat, pește fish, ou egg, ouă eggs. Corn on a Moldavian table is often păpușoi ; the standard word is porumb . That is a real regional split, listed also in the translator. pâine Bread. Heard as pâne in Moldavia and…

pages.title: 1. Greetings
pages.description: The hellos you actually say, and when each one is safe.
pages.text: Learn Romanian 1. Greetings The hellos you actually say, and when each one is safe. Start with bună ziua . It is good day, and it is the greeting that does not get you in trouble: morning, afternoon, a shop, a stranger. Bună is shorter and belongs with people you already know. Salut is informal. Bună dimineața is morning only. Seara bună or bună seara is evening. Noapte bună is for sleep, not for leaving a shop at 8. How are you is not a word-for-word copy of English. Ce faci? is what are you doing, said to one person you know, and it works as a hello. To a stranger or a group, ce faceți? The ordinary answer is bine, mulțumesc , then și tu? or și dumneavoastră? Names: cum te cheamă? is how are you called, which is what people ask. You can answer mă numesc… Leave-taking: la revedere until we see each other again; pa with friends; pe curând if it will be soon. bună ziua Good day. The safe…

pages.description: Rooms, the road, and which way to turn.
pages.text: Learn Romanian 4. House and directions Rooms, the road, and which way to turn. Casă is the house and also home. Acasă is at home. The rooms you need first: bucătărie kitchen, baie bathroom, cameră room, pat bed. Ușă is the door. Fereastră is the window; in Transylvania and Banat everyday speech often says geam for that opening, which the standard keeps for the pane. Outside: curte the yard, poartă the gate, fântână the well, drum the road. In town, stradă is the street and piață is the market or the square. Directions are short. La dreapta to the right, la stânga to the left, drept înainte straight on, aproape near, departe far. Asking: unde este…? or the spoken unde e…? pages.title: 2. Numbers and family
pages.description: Counting to ten, then the people in the house.
pages.text: Learn Romanian 2. Numbers and family Counting to ten, then the people in the house. One changes with the noun. Un bărbat , one man. O casă , one house. Two does the same: doi copii , două pâini . From three, the number stays put and the noun takes the plural. Ten is zece . Twenty is douăzeci . Age uses a avea: am douăzeci de ani , I have twenty years, which is how you say you are twenty. Family words are stable. Mamă and tată are the dictionary forms. What people say at the table is mama and tata . Frate , soră , bunic , bunică . The spoken grandparents are often bunicu and bunica . You is not one word. Tu is one person you know. Voi is more than one, still informal. Dumneavoastră is the polite you, singular or plural. The site uses it on purpose in shops and with elders. unu / un / o One. pages.title: 7. Polite forms
pages.description: Please, sorry, and the you that keeps distance.
pages.text: Learn Romanian 7. Polite forms Please, sorry, and the you that keeps distance. Vă rog is please to a stranger, a shop, an elder, or more than one person. Te rog is the same to someone you know. Both sit at the end of a request more often than at the start: o cafea, vă rog . Thank you is mulțumesc ; add mult for many thanks. The reply is cu plăcere , with pleasure, or nu-i nimic . Excuse me: scuzați in a crowd or to interrupt. Scuză-mă to a friend. Sorry for a real fault is îmi pare rău . Dumneavoastră takes plural verb forms even for one person: dumneavoastră sunteți , aveți , mergeți . That is the polite machinery. You do not mix tu with vă in the same address. Sărut mâna is still used to an older woman, literally I kiss your hand, as a hello. You can answer with a nod and bună ziua if you are not from here. Poftiți means come in, or here you are when something is handed over. vă rog…

pages.description: Tickets, the station, and the questions that get you there.
pages.text: Learn Romanian 6. Travel and asking Tickets, the station, and the questions that get you there. Question words sit at the front. Unde where, când when, cum how, cine who, ce what, de ce why, cât how much. Cât costă? is the price question. La ce oră? is at what time. Cât e ceasul? is what time is it. Travel nouns: bilet ticket, gară station, tren train, autobuz bus, aeroport airport, hotel hotel. Un bilet la București, vă rog is a full counter sentence. Vorbiți engleză? if you need to switch. Vorbesc puțin românește is honest and usually welcome. If you do not follow: nu înțeleg , then mai încet, vă rog and puteți repeta? Help is ajutor . The shout takes the same word. cât costă? pages.title: 5. Verbs in the present
pages.description: A few verbs you will live inside, with the forms you actually hear.
pages.text: Learn Romanian 5. Verbs in the present A few verbs you will live inside, with the forms you actually hear. Romanian dictionaries list verbs with a : a fi to be, a avea to have, a merge to go. That a is the infinitive marker. In a sentence you drop it and conjugate. A fi : eu sunt, tu ești, el/ea este (or e), noi suntem, voi sunteți, ei/ele sunt. In Moldavian speech, eu îs for eu sunt is common. A avea : am, ai, are, avem, aveți, au. Age, possession, and a lot of everyday need go through this verb. A merge is to go. Merg, mergi, merge, mergem, mergeți, merg. In Moldavia a umbla often does that job; in the standard, a umbla is closer to walk about. A vrea : vreau, vrei, vrea. Vreau apă is a full useful sentence. A putea : pot, poți, poate. Nu pot. A înțelege : înțeleg. Nu înțeleg is the one you will say most as a beginner. Oltenia still uses the simple past in ordinary speech — făcui…

pages.title: A century, read slowly
pages.description: The twentieth century here does not have one portrait. Read it as a sequence, and ask who is speaking.
pages.text: History A century, read slowly The twentieth century here does not have one portrait. Read it as a sequence, and ask who is speaking. A kingdom that had just become large spent the 1920s trying to govern lands that had never shared a law. Bucharest was the capital. Cluj, Chișinău, Cernăuți, and the Saxon towns had other memories. Land reform broke up some great estates and did not end village poverty. A constitution promised rights that parties, police, and local bosses applied unevenly. Jewish citizens faced exclusion that grew sharper as the European crisis deepened. None of this is a footnote to “what happened next.” It is the ground. In the 1930s the kingdom slid toward authoritarianism. King Carol II suspended ordinary politics. pages.title: Constanța
pages.description: A Greek town, a Roman exile, a port, and Romania’s window on the Black Sea.
pages.text: History Constanța A Greek town, a Roman exile, a port, and Romania’s window on the Black Sea. Imagined art — a waterfront, not a photograph of the casino Constanța sits on a low coast where the Dobruja meets the Black Sea. It is the country’s main seaport. The name people used for most of its ancient life was Tomis. Greek settlers from Miletus put a town here in the sixth century before the common era, one of a string of colonies along this shore. The sea was the street. Grain, fish, and later the traffic of empires moved through a harbor that is still the reason the city matters. The story almost everyone is told first is Ovid’s. The Roman poet was sent here in exile in the year 8, under Augustus, and he spent the rest of his life writing about the place as a cold edge of the world. pages.title: The Latin that stayed
pages.description: A short lesson on how a Roman province left a language behind.
pages.text: History The Latin that stayed A short lesson on how a Roman province left a language behind. Before the legions, the land inside and around the Carpathians was not empty and it was not “Romania.” Greek and later Roman writers knew a kingdom there, Dacia, and a people they called Dacians. Related groups lived south of the Danube, in what the same writers called Thrace. The names are older than any modern border. What matters for this lesson is simpler: a kingdom north of the river met an empire that wrote everything down, and the language of that empire did not leave when the soldiers did. Rome did not arrive all at once. There were raids, client arrangements, and then two hard wars under the emperor Trajan, in the first years of the second century. The Dacian king Decebalus was defeated. The capital, Sarmizegetusa, was taken. Dacia became a province, with forts, roads, mines, and…

pages.title: Why the walls are painted
pages.description: The churches of northern Moldavia were built to be read from the yard.
pages.text: History Why the walls are painted The churches of northern Moldavia were built to be read from the yard. A church in this part of the world is rarely only a church. In the villages of northern Moldavia, from the late fifteenth century into the sixteenth, princes and local patrons built small stone churches and then covered the outside walls with painting. The most famous stand near Suceava and in the valleys above it: Voroneț, Moldovița, Sucevița, Humor, Arbore. People now travel to see the color. The first audience was the people who lived there, many of whom did not read a book and did not need to. The wall was the book. The subjects are not decoration in the modern sense. There is a last judgment, a tree of Jesse, sieges, saints, and sometimes a scene of the siege of Constantinople. They sit in rows, like a procession you can walk. pages.title: Thrace and Dacia
pages.description: Two old names, often paired, and not the same kingdom.
pages.text: History Thrace and Dacia Two old names, often paired, and not the same kingdom. When the request came through for “thatchia and dathica,” the names that fit the history are Thrace and Dacia. They are easy to blur, because Greek and Roman writers often spoke of them in one breath, and because later national stories have wanted a single ancient ancestor. They were neighbors. They were not one court, and they did not leave one language we can still read. Thrace, to those writers, was the country north of the Aegean and mostly south of the Danube: the hills of what is now Bulgaria, parts of northern Greece, and European Turkey. Thracians appear in Homer as allies and as a people at the edge of the Greek world. Greek cities sat on their coast. A Thracian kingdom, the Odrysians, dealt with Athens and with Philip of Macedon. The language is almost gone. A handful of glosses, names, and…

pages.title: Three lands, not one court
pages.description: Wallachia, Moldavia, and Transylvania were neighbors for centuries before they were one state.
pages.text: History Three lands, not one court Wallachia, Moldavia, and Transylvania were neighbors for centuries before they were one state. If you look at a map of Romania today and then try to read a chronicle from the fifteenth century, the names will not line up. There was no single court ruling from the mountains to the sea. There were three political worlds, touching, trading, and fighting, and often paying tribute to a larger power that did not speak their language. Wallachia lay south of the Carpathians, between the mountains and the Danube. Its princes ruled from camps and then from towns, Târgoviște and later Bucharest among them. The land is a plain that rises into foothills. It looked south and east, toward the river and, for a long time, toward the Ottoman Empire. Tribute was not a metaphor. It was a payment that bought a kind of room to rule at home, and it could be raised, refused…

pages.title: How the country was put together
pages.description: The map people recognize is a nineteenth-century and early twentieth-century arrangement.
pages.text: History How the country was put together The map people recognize is a nineteenth-century and early twentieth-century arrangement. The Romanian state was not assembled by a single battle and a proclamation. It was assembled in stages, by elections, treaties, a war, and the collapse of empires that had sat on these lands for centuries. If you remember only one year, you will get the story wrong. 1859 and 1918 are the two hinges. They are not the same event. By the middle of the nineteenth century, Wallachia and Moldavia were still separate principalities, under Ottoman suzerainty and watched closely by Russia and by the other European powers. A generation of boyars and younger men who had studied in Paris wanted a constitution, a shared prince, and an end to being treated as a passageway. pages.text: Home Mărțișor March 1. A red-and-white thread on a coat, often with a small charm. Not a parade. The mark that winter is being argued with. Imagined art — the March thread on a branch, not a photograph What people pin The thing itself is small. Two strands twisted together — red and white — a șnur, pinned at the lapel or the collar. Often a charm hangs from it: a coin, a flower, a handmade figure someone sat with the night before. Shop versions glue a plastic snowdrop or a heart onto a card. The name covers the whole object, thread and trinket together. You wear it through early spring. When it comes off, the old habit is to hang it on a flowering tree or bush — a branch that has already opened — and leave it there. That is the end of the pin, not a ceremony with a ticket. pages.description: Schoolbooks lean on princes and a poet. The villages and the churches were still there when the princes died. These short notes name a few figures the lessons already brush past — not a single hero story.
pages.text: Home Men in Romania’s history Schoolbooks lean on princes and a poet. The villages and the churches were still there when the princes died. These short notes name a few figures the lessons already brush past — not a single hero story. Ștefan cel Mare Stephen the Great (Ștefan cel Mare) ruled Moldavia from 1457 to 1504. He fought the Ottomans and neighboring powers, won and lost in turn, and endowed churches across his land. Later national storytelling made him a pillar; the three lands lesson puts him back in a frontier principality, not a modern state. The exterior frescoes of northern Moldavia belong to his reign and the decades after it — see why the walls are painted . A painted church on a ridge was a claim that the feast days and the dead still had a place, not only a monument to one man. The creek at the edge of the sat, a race cut beside it, a wooden wheel that groaned when the sluice opened. The same water habit as rivers — the creek with no fame that still did a job. You heard it before you saw it: water, then wood, then stone. Some plains had a windmill; later a motor in a shed. The instruments people mean The nai is the pan flute: a row of pipes, shortest to longest, bound in a slight curve, played by blowing across the open ends. A shepherd’s nai was a smaller, less even instrument. The one on a record is usually the concert nai, built out in the twentieth century so it could follow a violin anywhere. Fănică Luca taught that modern instrument. Gheorghe Zamfir is the player most people outside the country have heard. Beautiful, and a little apart from the yard. You will still hear a nai in a band, but it is no longer the ordinary voice of a village afternoon. The fluier is the ordinary flute. Wood, a few finger holes, end-blown. This page is cultural memory — it does not speak for the Church. History here Christianity reached the lower Danube in the Roman centuries. Soldiers, traders, and settlers brought the faith into Dacia and along the Black Sea coast long before there was a Romanian state. The church that remained, north and south of the river, was the Eastern one: liturgy in Greek, then in Slavonic, bishops in communion with Constantinople rather than with the later Latin West. That Byzantine inheritance — chant, calendar, icons, and the shape of the Divine Liturgy — is still the ground under Romanian Orthodoxy, even after the language of worship became Romanian. A valley is often the river’s first, and the town sits where a bridge or a ford made sense. Imagined art — the Danube’s long reach Dunărea The Danube is the border and the highway at once. It comes in from the west, holds the south of the country for a long stretch, and then opens into the Delta before the Black Sea. Barges, ferries, and willow banks. In a dry summer the water drops and the islands grow. In a wet spring the low fields take the flood and people talk about it for years. Fishermen still work the quieter arms. The Delta is its own world — reeds, birds, houses on stilts — and it is not the same as the industrial river that passes Galati or the tourist stretch near the Iron Gates. Company that had a job in its lap. The room, not the hall A șezătoare is an evening of work in someone’s house — often the room by the stove, the one mapped on the house . You sit. You bring what your hands already know. Neighbors come because the lamp is on and the wool will not spin itself. Nobody stands at the front. It is not a concert and it is not school. The point is that the evening is long, so you do the work where there is talk. The word sits in the village the way a well or a gate does: ordinary, named, and easy to miss if you only look for feasts. A nuntă fills a yard; that day is on wedding .
